title: From strategy to execution: Arlande helps build the airport of the future - Consultancy.eu
description:
“Today, airports are complex mobility hubs where operations, technology and public interests all come together.” Arlande has evolved alongside this changing landscape.
While the firm’s roots lie firmly in airport operations, its role has expanded into broader consultancy support across the entire transformation journey.
By analysing passenger flows and identifying improvement opportunities, Arlande helps airports make better-informed decisions that enhance both efficiency and the passenger experience.
As passenger volumes continue to grow, efficient baggage handling remains a critical component of airport operations.
“This strengthens our ability to address complex airport challenges from multiple perspectives,” Jasper says.
text:
Over the past decades, airports have evolved from infrastructure-driven facilities into highly complex mobility ecosystems where technology, operations, passengers and public interests intersect. That transition is far from complete. The pressure to become more sustainable, the acceleration of digitalisation and increasingly demanding passenger expectations are pushing airports to rethink how they operate.

For more than 30 years, Arlande has been helping airports navigate their next phase of change – in the Netherlands and internationally. We spoke with Jasper Wildenberg (Lead Aviation International) and Kim de Graaf (Lead Aviation in the Netherlands) about the firm’s impact and the challenges shaping the industry’s future.

“Every day, I still look at aviation with amazement,” says Jasper. “The fact that humans are capable of making such enormous objects fly remains incredible.”

Jasper has spent the past eight years working in aviation through Arlande, and describes it as one of the most fascinating industries to operate in. “Few sectors are as complex as aviation. Safety, passenger experience, logistics, technology, services and public interests all come together. Every day presents a new puzzle: how can we make the aviation system work just a little better?”

Having been with Arlande and its predecessor Bostec for almost seven years, Kim shares that perspective. “What I enjoy most is the dynamics between all the different processes and stakeholders. The challenge is bringing all these parties together around one common objective: ensuring passengers can move through the airport as efficiently and comfortably as possible.”

For passengers, the complexity behind the scenes should ideally remain invisible. Yet for those working in aviation, it is precisely that complexity that makes the sector so compelling.

“Take baggage operations, for example,” says Jasper. “Walking through the baggage basement and seeing thousands of suitcases processed every day is fascinating. A combination of hardware, software and human coordination ensures that flights can depart on time – with the right baggage.”

From operational expertise to end-to-end consultancy

Over the past three decades, the challenges facing airports have changed significantly. “Thirty years ago, the focus was primarily on infrastructure and capacity,” Jasper explains. “Today, airports are complex mobility hubs where operations, technology and public interests all come together.”

Arlande has evolved alongside this changing landscape. While the firm’s roots lie firmly in airport operations, its role has expanded into broader consultancy support across the entire transformation journey.

“We have developed into a consultancy partner that supports airports end to end – from strategy and business cases through to implementation and operational optimisation,” says Jasper. “In a complex and highly regulated sector like aviation, having both strategic insight and the ability to execute is essential.”

This combination is increasingly important as airports face a continuous need to innovate while maintaining safe and reliable operations. “Airports are constantly being challenged to become smarter, more efficient and more future-proof,” Kim says. “At the same time, they operate 24/7 and safety always comes first. Finding the right balance between innovation and operational excellence is therefore a major challenge.”

This development is also changing the role of external partners. Rather than simply delivering solutions, suppliers are increasingly expected to act as strategic partners. “The organisations that create the most value are those that are transparent, share knowledge and actively contribute to strengthening the airport organisation itself,” Kim explains.

Schiphol in Amsterdam is one of Arlande’s clients in the sector

Four priorities shaping the future of airports

To support airports in their transformation journeys, Arlande focuses on four key themes that are expected to define the sector in the years ahead.

The first is optimising passenger processes. By analysing passenger flows and identifying improvement opportunities, Arlande helps airports make better-informed decisions that enhance both efficiency and the passenger experience.

“Improving passenger flow is not only about speed,” Jasper explains. “It is about creating a smoother, more predictable journey. We have, for example, contributed to the development of the seamless flow concept and supported the testing and optimisation of self-service passport control.”

A second focus area is smart baggage. As passenger volumes continue to grow, efficient baggage handling remains a critical component of airport operations.

“We have colleagues with more than 20 years of experience in the baggage domain,” Kim says. “Their knowledge allows us to advise airports on strategic choices while also helping improve day-to-day operations through better control systems, automation and robotics.”

The third theme is innovation and sustainability – two areas that are increasingly intertwined.

“Sustainability challenges require innovation, and innovation must ultimately contribute to a more sustainable aviation system,” Jasper says. “We support airports in exploring, assessing and implementing new solutions while considering the impact on operations, the organisation and the longer term.”

One example is a project involving autonomous wheelchairs that help passengers with reduced mobility reach their departure gates. “This demonstrates how innovation is not just about technology,” Jasper explains. “It can also improve accessibility, reliability and the overall passenger experience.”

The fourth theme is integrated planning and operations: creating stronger connections between planning processes and daily execution.

“When planning and operations are better aligned, airports gain more control over disruptions, capacity challenges and operational decision-making,” Kim says. “For example, we supported the project and testing management for a temporary departure hall – a critical initiative to maintain capacity.”

Combining expertise

While each theme addresses a specific challenge, they are often closely connected. To provide a broader offering, Arlande collaborates with sister company VFM Facility Experts and DAAV, a provider of inclusive mobility solutions.

“This strengthens our ability to address complex airport challenges from multiple perspectives,” Jasper says. “VFM brings expertise in facility management, airport assets and contracts, while DAAV provides autonomous mobility solutions for passengers with reduced mobility.”

DAAV and Arlande are driving the adoption of inclusive mobility solutions at airports

The result is an integrated approach rather than a collection of separate solutions. “For clients, this means working with one coordinated team instead of multiple specialists,” Jasper explains. “Together, we can deliver solutions that work at strategic, tactical and operational levels.”

Expanding beyond the Netherlands

As aviation itself is an international industry, Arlande’s expertise is increasingly reaching beyond Dutch borders. Under Jasper’s leadership, the firm is expanding its international aviation activities, particularly around passenger and baggage processes.

“We are increasingly involved in international airport programmes,” he says. “Our experience with major European hubs allows us to quickly understand complex operational challenges and identify practical solutions.”

A key challenge facing airports, he says, is moving beyond experimentation. “Many airports remain stuck in pilots. The real challenge is making choices, setting priorities and moving towards implementation.”

One example is Arlande’s support for an international airport in developing a sourcing and operating model strategy for cleaning services. The team contributed not only sector expertise, but also support around governance and procurement. “Every airport requires a tailored approach,” Jasper explains. “Local circumstances, regulations and organisational maturity all influence what works best.”

The firm’s international ambitions are selective rather than based on the volume of projects. “Our goal is not simply to operate in as many countries as possible,” Jasper says. “We want to be active where our expertise genuinely adds value. Our ambition is to be recognised internationally as a trusted partner that combines proven airport experience with pragmatism and strong implementation capability.”

Helping airports make the right choices

In the Netherlands, Kim leads Arlande’s continued focus on supporting airports through an increasingly complex environment. “In the coming years, we want to help airports make well-informed choices about where they should invest and what will truly create value,” she says. “That is not simply about introducing new technology. It is about understanding what makes a meaningful difference today and in the future.”

Jasper agrees that successful innovation requires more than ideas. “In aviation, innovation is often not about inventing something completely new. It is about successfully scaling solutions that have already demonstrated their value,” he says. “Many airports remain in pilot mode. The real added value of consultancy lies in helping organisations make choices, prioritise and implement.”

A partner embedded in the organisation

This practical approach is central to Arlande’s identity, Kim says. “We combine deep sector expertise with practical understanding of airport processes. That means solutions are not only designed, but also implemented successfully and embraced by the organisation.”

She adds that Arlande deliberately works shoulder to shoulder with its clients. “You will not always notice us as consultants because we become part of the organisation. At the same time, we make sure knowledge is transferred and embedded. Being an independent, knowledgeable and genuinely involved partner is what defines us.”

For Kim, successful transformation ultimately comes down to collaboration. “I believe progress happens when everyone understands that they are working towards the same goal, even when different interests are involved. When we can create that shared sense of purpose across projects and organisations, that is when collaboration truly succeeds.”

text:
Hong Kong – 10July2026 – EcoCeres, a global leader in the innovation and commercialization of renewable fuels and green molecules, announced that it will supply sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) to Viva Energy Australia (Viva Energy), one of Australia’s leading energy companies, for storage and distribution through Viva Energy’s Pinkenba fuel terminal in Brisbane, Queensland.

Viva Energy’s Pinkenba SAF infrastructure project, supported by funding from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA), has been designed to demonstrate the delivery of SAF through existing fuel supply infrastructure to Brisbane Airport and beyond.

Matti Lievonen, CEO of EcoCeres said: “Partnering with Viva Energy to further expand the availability of our SAF in the Australian market is an important milestone in EcoCeres’ growth journey and in the broader decarbonization of aviation in this region. By supplying SAF to Viva Energy, we are able to connect our production capabilities with established storage and distribution infrastructure, helping airlines access low‑carbon fuel at scale through familiar supply chains.” He added, “Australia is a key growth market for sustainable fuels, and we look forward to working with Viva Energy and its customers to turn net‑zero ambitions into concrete emissions reductions in the years ahead.”

The collaboration between EcoCeres and Viva Energy will help lay the foundation for a more mature SAF ecosystem in Australia by demonstrating how existing terminal infrastructure can be used for SAF storage, blending and distribution, while providing airlines with access to certified waste‑based SAF without requiring changes to aircraft or airport refueling infrastructure, and creating a platform for future initiatives such as book‑and‑claim systems and broader regional supply chains for low‑carbon liquid fuels.

title: Aircraft Fuel Systems Market Size, Share & Forecast 2026–2033
description:
Airlines worldwide are replacing older aircraft with more fuel-efficient platforms that incorporate advanced aircraft fuel management systems, lightweight fuel tanks, digitally integrated fuel quantity indication systems, fuel monitoring technologies, and high-efficiency fuel pumps and valves.
Aircraft Fuel Systems Market Trends & Opportunities Digital Aircraft Fuel Management and Predictive Health Monitoring Digitalization is emerging as a major trend across the aircraft fuel systems market as airlines increasingly adopt intelligent aircraft fuel management systems capable of improving operational efficiency, maintenance planning, and fuel utilization.
Aircraft fuel systems—including fuel tanks, fuel pumps, valves, fuel quantity indication systems, fuel management systems, and fuel distribution networks—are essential for ensuring safe fuel storage, accurate fuel monitoring, efficient fuel transfer, and reliable engine performance throughout flight operations.
Rising passenger traffic, expanding airline fleets, and growing aircraft production are generating substantial demand for aircraft fuel systems, fuel distribution systems, fuel pumps, aircraft fuel tanks, and advanced fuel monitoring technologies.
Leading Middle Eastern airlines continue investing in next-generation commercial aircraft to support long-haul international operations, generating demand for advanced aircraft fuel systems, fuel management systems, fuel quantity indication systems, and fuel distribution technologies.
text:
Overview

The global aircraft fuel systems market was valued at US$ 9.7 billion in 2025 and is expected to reach US$ 12.5 billion by 2033, growing at a CAGR of 3.1% during the forecast period 2026–2033. Aircraft fuel systems are critical to aircraft performance and safety, comprising integrated components such as fuel tanks, pumps, valves, filters, pipelines, sensors, fuel quantity indication systems, and fuel management technologies that ensure the safe storage, transfer, monitoring, and delivery of fuel to aircraft engines. As airlines and aircraft manufacturers continue to prioritize fuel efficiency, operational reliability, and lifecycle cost reduction, demand is increasing for more intelligent fuel management systems capable of supporting digital monitoring, predictive maintenance, and optimized fuel utilization. The aviation industry's broader digital transformation is also accelerating the adoption of standardized fuel data management and analytics to improve operational efficiency throughout the fuel supply chain and aircraft operations. Recent initiatives such as the International Air Transport Association's (IATA) FuelIS analytics platform and Fuel Data Standards further demonstrate the industry's increasing focus on digital fuel management and operational optimization.

The market is also being reshaped by the rapid expansion of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) adoption as airlines, aircraft manufacturers, and governments pursue long-term decarbonization goals. Although SAF is designed as a drop-in fuel compatible with existing aircraft, its growing commercial deployment is driving additional validation, testing, certification, and optimization of aircraft fuel handling, storage, metering, and monitoring systems to ensure reliable operation across a wider range of approved fuel blends. According to IATA, sustainable aviation fuel is expected to contribute approximately 65% of the emissions reductions required for aviation to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2050, reinforcing continued investment in SAF-compatible aircraft technologies and supporting infrastructure.

Beyond SAF, aircraft manufacturers and aerospace suppliers are accelerating research into next-generation propulsion technologies, particularly liquid hydrogen-powered aircraft, which require fundamentally different fuel storage, transfer, thermal management, and pressure control systems compared with conventional aviation fuels. Reflecting this long-term transition, Airbus, Parker Hannifin, Marshall, and GKN Aerospace announced collaborations during 2024 to advance hydrogen fuel system technologies through the HyFIVE consortium, supporting the development of zero-emission aircraft expected in the next decade. While hydrogen aviation remains at an early stage of commercialization, continued investment in advanced fuel system architectures is expanding innovation opportunities and strengthening the long-term outlook for the global aircraft fuel systems market.

Drivers

Rising Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) Adoption Driving Demand for Compatible Aircraft Fuel Systems

The increasing adoption of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is a major driver for the aircraft fuel systems market as the aviation industry accelerates efforts to reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions while continuing to utilize existing aircraft fleets. Although SAF is approved as a drop-in replacement for conventional jet fuel within certified blending limits, expanding its commercial use requires extensive qualification of aircraft fuel management systems, fuel pumps, valves, seals, filters, fuel quantity indication systems, and fuel control components to ensure long-term compatibility, material integrity, and operational reliability. Aircraft OEMs and fuel system manufacturers are therefore investing in component validation, testing, and certification programs to support increasing SAF utilization across commercial and military aviation.

Commercial deployment of SAF continues to accelerate globally. According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), global SAF production is expected to reach approximately 2 million tonnes (around 2.5 billion litres) in 2025, representing more than a two-fold increase compared with 2024 production. Although this still accounts for less than 1% of total global aviation fuel consumption, the rapid expansion in production capacity is encouraging airlines and aircraft manufacturers to prepare fleets for broader SAF adoption through continued investment in compatible aircraft fuel system technologies.

Aircraft manufacturers are also progressing toward higher SAF utilization. Airbus has stated that all of its commercial aircraft are currently certified to operate using up to 50% SAF blends and is working with engine manufacturers and fuel suppliers to support operation using 100% SAF before 2030. As airlines progressively increase SAF usage to meet decarbonization commitments and regulatory targets, demand for advanced aircraft fuel management systems, fuel distribution systems, fuel monitoring systems, and high-performance fuel handling components is expected to grow steadily throughout the forecast period.

Growing Aircraft Production and Fleet Modernization Supporting OEM and Aftermarket Demand

Growing commercial aircraft production and fleet modernization programs are significantly driving demand for aircraft fuel systems across both OEM and aftermarket channels. Airlines worldwide are replacing older aircraft with more fuel-efficient platforms that incorporate advanced aircraft fuel management systems, lightweight fuel tanks, digitally integrated fuel quantity indication systems, fuel monitoring technologies, and high-efficiency fuel pumps and valves. These next-generation systems improve operational reliability, optimize fuel consumption, and reduce maintenance requirements while supporting compliance with increasingly stringent aviation safety and environmental standards.

The industry's exceptionally large aircraft backlog provides strong long-term visibility for fuel system suppliers. According to Airbus, the company reported a commercial aircraft backlog exceeding 8,700 aircraft at the end of 2025, while Boeing's commercial backlog remained above 6,000 aircraft. Every new aircraft delivered requires complete fuel storage, transfer, monitoring, filtration, and control systems, creating sustained demand for aircraft fuel system manufacturers throughout the production lifecycle.

Beyond new aircraft production, the expanding global fleet is generating substantial recurring revenue through aftermarket maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) activities. Aircraft fuel pumps, valves, sensors, filters, fuel lines, and fuel quantity indication systems require periodic inspection, replacement, calibration, and certification throughout an aircraft's operational life. As global passenger traffic continues to recover and airlines increase aircraft utilization, demand for aftermarket aircraft fuel system components and MRO services is expected to remain a major contributor to long-term market growth.

Restraint

Lengthy Certification Requirements and Complex Aerospace Supply Chains

Lengthy certification processes and complex aerospace supply chains remain significant restraints on the aircraft fuel systems market. Aircraft fuel systems are classified as safety-critical equipment and therefore must comply with rigorous certification requirements established by aviation authorities including the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), and other national regulators. New fuel pumps, valves, sensors, electronic fuel management systems, and integrated fuel control components must undergo extensive laboratory qualification, environmental testing, vibration testing, electromagnetic compatibility assessment, flight validation, and reliability demonstration before receiving airworthiness approval. These extensive validation procedures increase development costs and extend commercialization timelines for new technologies.

The market is further constrained by dependence on highly specialized aerospace suppliers that manufacture precision valves, sensors, actuators, electronic controllers, filtration systems, and advanced sealing materials. Supply disruptions affecting titanium, nickel alloys, electronic components, and aerospace-grade castings continue to extend lead times for aircraft production and replacement parts. According to Airbus' 2025 Full-Year Results, persistent supply chain challenges remained one of the principal factors affecting aircraft production and delivery schedules, illustrating how upstream manufacturing constraints continue to influence demand across the broader aircraft fuel systems supply chain.

Aircraft Fuel Systems Market Trends & Opportunities

Digital Aircraft Fuel Management and Predictive Health Monitoring

Digitalization is emerging as a major trend across the aircraft fuel systems market as airlines increasingly adopt intelligent aircraft fuel management systems capable of improving operational efficiency, maintenance planning, and fuel utilization. Modern aircraft fuel systems increasingly integrate electronic sensors, fuel quantity indication systems, flow monitoring devices, and onboard diagnostics that provide continuous operational data to flight crews and maintenance teams. These technologies enable predictive maintenance, reduce unscheduled component failures, improve fuel efficiency, and enhance aircraft dispatch reliability while lowering lifecycle operating costs.

Supporting this trend, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) continues to expand its FuelIS platform and Fuel Data Standards, enabling airlines to analyze fuel consumption, benchmark operational performance, and identify fuel-saving opportunities using standardized digital data. As airlines continue investing in digital fleet management and operational analytics, demand for intelligent aircraft fuel monitoring systems and digitally connected fuel management technologies is expected to increase steadily.

Hydrogen Propulsion Accelerating Innovation in Next-Generation Aircraft Fuel Systems

The growing development of hydrogen-powered aircraft is driving innovation in next-generation aircraft fuel systems capable of handling cryogenic liquid hydrogen and other zero-emission propulsion technologies. Unlike conventional jet fuel, liquid hydrogen requires specialized storage tanks, advanced thermal insulation, pressure regulation systems, cryogenic valves, and highly sophisticated fuel transfer technologies. These engineering requirements are encouraging aerospace manufacturers to redesign aircraft fuel system architectures for future aircraft platforms.

Industry collaboration continues to accelerate technology development. In 2024, Parker Aerospace joined Marshall, GKN Aerospace, and other partners within the HyFIVE consortium to develop liquid hydrogen fuel system technologies supporting future zero-emission aviation. Although hydrogen-powered commercial aircraft remain under development, these investments are expanding research into advanced aircraft fuel tanks, cryogenic fuel management systems, thermal control technologies, and next-generation fuel distribution systems, creating long-term opportunities for suppliers across the aircraft fuel systems market.

Segment Analysis

The global aircraft fuel systems industry is segmented based on system, technology, engine type, aircraft type, point of sale and by region.

Fleet Expansion and Aircraft Modernization Sustain Commercial Aviation Leadership

The commercial aviation segment accounted for approximately 56.4% of the global aircraft fuel systems market in 2025, making it the largest aircraft type segment. Its dominance is supported by continuous fleet expansion, rising aircraft production, and sustained investments in fuel-efficient commercial aircraft. Aircraft fuel systems—including fuel tanks, fuel pumps, valves, fuel quantity indication systems, fuel management systems, and fuel distribution networks—are essential for ensuring safe fuel storage, accurate fuel monitoring, efficient fuel transfer, and reliable engine performance throughout flight operations. Airlines are increasingly adopting advanced aircraft fuel systems that improve fuel efficiency, reduce maintenance requirements, and support compatibility with sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

Long-term aircraft production forecasts continue to reinforce demand for OEM aircraft fuel systems. According to Airbus' Global Market Forecast 2024, approximately 42,430 new passenger and freighter aircraft will be required globally by 2043. Similarly, Boeing's Commercial Market Outlook 2024 projects demand for over 43,900 new commercial airplanes during the same period. Continued aircraft deliveries, fleet replacement programs, increasing passenger traffic, and growing adoption of digital fuel management technologies are expected to sustain commercial aviation's leadership throughout the forecast period.

Global Defense Modernization Programs Fuel Military Aviation Growth

Military aviation is projected to register the fastest growth throughout the forecast period owing to increasing defense modernization programs, rising procurement of fighter aircraft, transport aircraft, helicopters, and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Modern military platforms require highly specialized aircraft fuel systems capable of operating under extreme temperatures, high-G maneuvers, aerial refueling operations, and extended mission durations while maintaining operational reliability and aircraft survivability.

According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), global military expenditure reached a record US$2.72 trillion in 2024, representing a 9.4% increase compared with 2023. Rising defense budgets are accelerating investments in next-generation combat aircraft equipped with lightweight fuel tanks, crash-resistant fuel storage systems, digital fuel monitoring, and advanced fuel tank inerting technologies. These modernization initiatives are expected to significantly increase demand for advanced military aircraft fuel systems.

Large Installed Aircraft Fleet Continues to Support Conventional Engine Dominance

Conventional engines accounted for approximately 95% of the aircraft fuel systems market in 2025 due to the extensive global fleet of turbofan, turboprop, turboshaft, and piston-powered aircraft. Commercial airlines, military operators, business aviation fleets, and regional carriers continue to rely primarily on conventional propulsion systems supported by mature aircraft fuel management technologies.

Although hybrid-electric propulsion is gaining industry attention, the overwhelming majority of new aircraft deliveries during the forecast period are expected to utilize conventional engines. Their established certification standards, global maintenance infrastructure, and proven operational reliability continue to sustain demand for conventional aircraft fuel systems across both OEM and aftermarket channels. Hybrid-electric aircraft remain primarily in demonstration and developmental phases, limiting current commercial revenue contribution.

Next-Generation Aircraft Propulsion Technologies Drive Hybrid-Electric Adoption

Hybrid-electric propulsion is expected to be the fastest-growing engine segment as the aviation industry accelerates development of lower-emission aircraft technologies. Aircraft manufacturers are actively evaluating hybrid-electric propulsion architectures to improve fuel efficiency, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and support future sustainability objectives.

Programs such as Airbus' ZEROe initiative and multiple regional aircraft demonstration projects are driving development of integrated fuel management systems capable of supporting both conventional fuel and electric propulsion technologies. As hybrid-electric aircraft progress toward commercialization, demand for next-generation aircraft fuel systems with advanced control, monitoring, and energy management capabilities is expected to grow steadily.

Increasing Focus on Fuel Efficiency and System Reliability Sustains Fuel Supply & Distribution Leadership

Fuel Supply & Distribution Systems represented approximately 43% of the global aircraft fuel systems market in 2025. This segment includes fuel pumps, valves, fuel injectors, filters, pipelines, hoses, and associated fuel control components responsible for delivering fuel safely and efficiently to aircraft engines under varying flight conditions.

The segment continues to benefit from increasing aircraft production, fleet modernization, and growing emphasis on operational efficiency. Aircraft manufacturers are investing in lightweight fuel distribution systems, digitally monitored fuel flow technologies, and improved fuel control architectures that enhance aircraft performance while supporting compatibility with sustainable aviation fuels.

Enhanced Aircraft Safety Standards Accelerate Fuel Tank Inerting System Deployment

Fuel Tank Inerting Systems are projected to witness the fastest growth during the forecast period owing to increasing emphasis on aircraft safety and regulatory compliance. These systems reduce oxygen concentration inside aircraft fuel tanks through nitrogen-enriched air generation, significantly minimizing ignition risk during flight operations.

Growing integration of inert gas generation systems into commercial aircraft, military aircraft, and next-generation aviation platforms is supporting market growth. Continued emphasis on flight safety, fuel tank explosion prevention, and evolving aircraft certification requirements is expected to accelerate adoption of advanced fuel tank inerting technologies worldwide.

Reliable Fuel Delivery Across Modern Aircraft Platforms Supports Pump Feed System Dominance

Pump Feed Systems accounted for approximately 68% of the aircraft fuel systems market in 2025 due to their widespread deployment across commercial aircraft, military aircraft, helicopters, and business jets. These systems provide consistent fuel pressure regardless of aircraft attitude, altitude, or maneuvering conditions, making them indispensable for modern turbine-powered aircraft.

Increasing aircraft production, growing fleet utilization, and continuous improvements in fuel pump efficiency, reliability, and digital monitoring capabilities continue to strengthen demand for pump feed systems across both OEM and replacement markets.

Geographical Penetration

North America Aircraft Fuel Systems Market: Driven by SAF Commercialization and Advanced Aircraft Development

North America accounted for approximately 43.2% of the global aircraft fuel systems market in 2025, supported by its strong aircraft manufacturing ecosystem, continuous investment in aviation technologies, and leadership in sustainable aviation initiatives. The region is home to major aircraft OEMs, engine manufacturers, and aircraft system suppliers, creating sustained demand for advanced aircraft fuel systems, fuel management systems, fuel pumps, valves, sensors, and fuel monitoring technologies across both commercial and military aviation.

Government policy continues to strengthen market growth. The U.S. Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) Grand Challenge targets production of 3 billion gallons of SAF annually by 2030 and 35 billion gallons by 2050, accelerating industry investment in SAF-compatible aircraft fuel systems. At the same time, manufacturers are preparing for future propulsion technologies. In April 2024, Parker Aerospace joined the HyFIVE consortium to support development of liquid hydrogen fuel systems for next-generation aircraft, reinforcing North America's position as a leading center for aircraft fuel system innovation. Combined with strong MRO activity, aircraft fleet renewal, and continued commercial aircraft production, these factors continue to drive the regional aircraft fuel systems market.

Europe Aircraft Fuel Systems Market: Driven by Aviation Decarbonization and Next-Generation Propulsion Innovation

Europe represents a significant aircraft fuel systems market owing to ambitious decarbonization policies, continuous aerospace innovation, and increasing investment in sustainable aircraft technologies. Aircraft manufacturers, engine suppliers, and system integrators across the region are accelerating development of fuel-efficient aircraft platforms while advancing aircraft fuel management systems capable of supporting sustainable aviation fuels and future hydrogen-powered aircraft.

The European Union continues to strengthen aviation decarbonization through ReFuelEU Aviation, which mandates increasing SAF supply at EU airports beginning in 2025 and progressively raising blending requirements through 2050. These regulatory measures are encouraging airlines, OEMs, and fuel system manufacturers to accelerate development of SAF-compatible aircraft fuel tanks, pumps, valves, fuel metering units, and monitoring systems. Alongside SAF adoption, European aerospace companies continue investing in hydrogen aircraft research, digital aircraft systems, and lightweight fuel storage technologies, supporting long-term growth of the aircraft fuel systems industry.

Asia-Pacific Aircraft Fuel Systems Market: Driven by Record Aircraft Deliveries and Expanding Aerospace Manufacturing

Asia-Pacific is projected to register the fastest growth during the forecast period, driven by rapidly expanding commercial aviation, rising defense procurement, and increasing domestic aerospace manufacturing capabilities. Rising passenger traffic, expanding airline fleets, and growing aircraft production are generating substantial demand for aircraft fuel systems, fuel distribution systems, fuel pumps, aircraft fuel tanks, and advanced fuel monitoring technologies.

According to Airbus' Global Market Forecast 2024, Asia-Pacific will account for the largest share of global aircraft deliveries over the next two decades as airlines continue expanding capacity to meet rising passenger demand. India and China are also investing heavily in indigenous aerospace manufacturing while strengthening commercial aviation infrastructure. At the same time, countries including Japan, South Korea, Australia, and India continue modernizing military aircraft fleets, increasing demand for advanced military aircraft fuel systems, crash-resistant fuel tanks, and fuel tank inerting technologies. Growing aircraft production, expanding MRO infrastructure, and increasing OEM investment are expected to sustain strong regional growth.

South America Aircraft Fuel Systems Market: Supported by Fleet Renewal and Expanding Commercial Aviation

The South America aircraft fuel systems market is experiencing steady growth as airlines modernize aging fleets and regional air travel continues recovering. Commercial aircraft operators across Brazil, Chile, Colombia, and Argentina are investing in newer fuel-efficient aircraft that require advanced aircraft fuel systems capable of improving operational efficiency while supporting future sustainable aviation fuel adoption.

Brazil continues to strengthen its position as the region's aerospace manufacturing hub through Embraer's commercial, executive, and defense aircraft production. In parallel, governments and airlines are increasing investment in aviation infrastructure and fleet modernization programs to improve connectivity across the continent. Growing aircraft deliveries, increasing maintenance activities, and expanding aftermarket demand for aircraft fuel pumps, valves, filters, sensors, and fuel management systems are expected to support continued growth of the South American aircraft fuel systems market.

Middle East & Africa Aircraft Fuel Systems Market: Driven by Airline Expansion and Military Aviation Investments

The Middle East & Africa aircraft fuel systems market is growing steadily due to ongoing airline fleet expansion, increasing defense aviation investments, and continued development of regional aviation infrastructure. Leading Middle Eastern airlines continue investing in next-generation commercial aircraft to support long-haul international operations, generating demand for advanced aircraft fuel systems, fuel management systems, fuel quantity indication systems, and fuel distribution technologies.

The region also remains a major defense aviation market, with countries including Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar investing in advanced fighter aircraft, transport aircraft, helicopters, and military support platforms. According to SIPRI, the Middle East remains one of the world's highest defense spending regions relative to GDP, supporting sustained procurement of modern military aircraft equipped with sophisticated fuel storage, fuel transfer, and fuel monitoring systems. Simultaneously, expansion of regional MRO capabilities and increasing adoption of fuel-efficient aircraft are expected to strengthen long-term demand for aircraft fuel systems across the Middle East & Africa.

Key Developments

·In April 2026, Eaton signed an agreement with Air Support to provide local repair and support for Eaton’s engine fuel components for large commercial aircraft. Under the agreement, Air Support became the first authorized service center for Eaton’s aerospace business across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa, significantly expanding Eaton’s aftermarket fuel system service network and improving maintenance accessibility for commercial aircraft operators across the region.

·In March 2025, the first sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) delivery took place at the Airbus Canada's A220 site, enabling the Mirabel teams to use SAF for production, customer acceptance and test flights. This now means that all Airbus commercial aircraft assembly sites around the world are now using sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) for their internal operations. During the course of 2025, all Airbus commercial aircraft delivery centers around the world will offer SAF to customers for ferry flights. This year alone, in 2025, over 600,000 litres of SAF with a 30% blend are expected to be used at the Airbus Mirabel site resulting in a reduction in CO2 emissions of around 400 metric tons.
